questions.question: How does Constellation Energy's disclosed view of nuclear fuel supply risk differ from Cameco's discussion of uranium supply risk, given their different positions in the nuclear fuel supply chain?
questions.golden_answer: Constellation Energy (a nuclear utility / fuel buyer) states in its FY2023 10-K that it 'does not anticipate difficulty' obtaining the uranium concentrates, conversion, enrichment, or fabrication services it needs, framing fuel procurement as a manageable, diversified-supplier risk. Cameco (a uranium producer/miner) instead describes deep producer-side geopolitical supply risk in its FY2025 AIF -- citing the Russian invasion of Ukraine, the 2024 Niger mine suspension, Kazakhstan supply-chain challenges, and sanctions/import-export restrictions as factors causing governments and utilities to re-examine sourcing from higher-risk jurisdictions.

agent.answer:
Constellation Energy describes nuclear fuel supply risk from the perspective of a nuclear fleet operator that needs fuel to keep reactors running. Its filings say it obtains fuel through long-term uranium concentrate, conversion, enrichment, and fabrication contracts; maintains inventories in various forms; uses a diverse set of domestic and international suppliers; limits transactions with each supplier to reduce concentration risk; and sizes inventory and forward contractual coverage across multiple years to protect against supply disruptions and near-term price volatility. In 2023 it said it did not anticipate difficulty obtaining the uranium concentrates and related services needed for its fleet, and in 2024 it said it was using “all available avenues” and working with the U.S. government and suppliers to ensure long-term continuity of supply [CEG_2023_10-K_0079] [CEG_2024_10-K_0070]. At the same time, Constellation acknowledges procurement risk: nuclear fuel markets are subject to price fluctuations, availability restrictions, counterparty default, and geopolitical risk, including Russia-related sanctions and import bans that can affect Russian nuclear fuel [CEG_2023_10-K_0104] [CEG_2025_10-K_0078].

Cameco discusses uranium supply risk from the perspective of an upstream fuel-cycle supplier. It says future uranium and nuclear fuel supply is not keeping pace with rising demand, and attributes heightened supply risk to geopolitical uncertainty, shrinking secondary supplies, and a lack of investment in new capacity over the past decade [CCJ_2023_40-F_0340] [CCJ_2024_40-F_0353] [CCJ_2025_40-F_0348]. Cameco emphasizes that this uncertainty is motivating utilities to re-evaluate near-, mid-, and long-term fuel supply chains and to increase long-term contracting, while competition to secure uranium, conversion, and enrichment under long-term contracts is expected to continue [CCJ_2023_40-F_0340] [CCJ_2024_40-F_0353] [CCJ_2025_40-F_0348]. It further states that geopolitical events, sanctions, insurance cancellations, and transportation issues have shifted risk from producers to utilities [CCJ_2023_40-F_0345], while Cameco portrays itself as a “proven and reliable supplier” with diversified production, market-sourcing options, inventory, storage, and purchase arrangements that position it to benefit from added demand and higher prices [CCJ_2023_40-F_0350].

So the difference is that Constellation frames nuclear fuel supply risk mainly as a procurement-and-continuity risk to an end-user utility, managed through diversification, inventory, and long-term coverage, whereas Cameco frames uranium supply risk mainly as a structural market shortfall and geopolitical supply uncertainty in the upstream fuel chain that is driving utility contracting demand and benefiting reliable suppliers like Cameco [CEG_2023_10-K_0079] [CEG_2024_10-K_0070] [CEG_2023_10-K_0104] [CEG_2025_10-K_0078] [CCJ_2023_40-F_0340] [CCJ_2024_40-F_0353] [CCJ_2025_40-F_0348] [CCJ_2023_40-F_0345] [CCJ_2023_40-F_0350].
